belief: “The people I love will eventually leave me.”
belief_plain: The people I love will eventually leave me.
intro: Do you often brace for the moment someone you care about walks away? Does a delayed text or a change in tone make your heart sink? The information below is intended to help you take a step toward feeling more secure, and to find the steadiness that comes from knowing God’s word as found in the Bible.
origins: This fear often grows out of real loss: a parent who left or was emotionally absent, a divorce, a death, a betrayal, or a friend who disappeared. When people we needed did leave, the mind learns to expect it. Scanning for signs of leaving can feel like protection, though it often wears out the very relationships we want to keep.
keeps: If I expect to be left, I may cling, test people, pull away first, or read ordinary changes as proof. Others can feel pressure or confusion, and sometimes step back, which seems to confirm the fear. Meanwhile the many people who stayed are easy to overlook.
teaches: Scripture does not promise that people will never disappoint us, but it does promise that God does not leave. “He will never leave you nor forsake you.” Even in the worst loss, “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me.” Christ told His followers, “I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you.” Our security rests first on a love that cannot be lost, which then lets us love people without gripping them.
key: The LORD Himself goes before you; He will be with you. He will never leave you nor forsake you. Do not be afraid or discouraged.
also: Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me.
I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you.

For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
self: I cannot count on anyone to stay.
It is only a matter of time.
If I get close, I will be hurt.
errors: Predicting that people will leave before there is evidence.
Turning one or two losses into “everyone leaves.”
Assuming a quiet or busy moment means someone is done with me.
Treating any distance as complete abandonment.
Feeling afraid and concluding the loss is coming.
Overlooking the people who have stayed.
questions: Who has stayed with me, and for how long?
What is the actual evidence that this person is leaving?
Are there other explanations for the delay or distance?
Do I treat one painful loss as proof about everyone?
What does Scripture say about God’s presence with me?
How do my fear-driven actions affect my relationships?
If a friend feared this, what would I say to them?
truth: Some people have left me, but that does not mean everyone will. God will never leave me, and my security rests in His love. I can care about people without gripping them, and I can face any loss with Him beside me.
prayer: Lord, thank You that You will never leave me. Calm the fear of being left, steady my heart in Your love, and help me to love others freely without clinging. Amen.
clinical: For counselors: this belief appears in the cognitive model of what clinicians call borderline personality disorder (Beck, Davis, & Freeman, Cognitive Therapy of Personality Disorders), where fear of abandonment, all-or-nothing thinking about people, an unsettled sense of self, and a fear of being overwhelmed by emotion are central. Fear of abandonment typically traces to early loss or unstable caregiving; assess attachment history, current relational triggers, and how the person responds (clinging, testing, or withdrawing first). Behavioral skills for tolerating distress and regulating emotion (as in Linehan’s DBT) pair well with this card’s Identify → Challenge → Replace work. Screen for self-harm and suicide risk, and consult or refer when risk is present (in the U.S., 988). This is an individualized educational formulation, not a DSM criterion or a diagnostic test. Similar presentations can arise from trauma, depression, anxiety, or temperament, so careful assessment matters. Pace any experiments to the person.
morning: Each morning ask: “Who has stayed with me, and how is God with me today?”
hw_truths: A delay is not a departure.
My security rests in God’s love.
I can face a loss with God beside me.
experiments: List the people who have stayed in your life, and thank one of them.
When you fear someone is pulling away, write three other possible explanations before reacting.
Wait one hour before sending a reassurance-seeking message, and note what happens.
Tell a safe person about your fear instead of testing them.
Pray Deuteronomy 31:8 aloud when the fear rises.
Notice and record each time a person you care about follows through.
reflect: After listening to one of the four songs, write a sentence about God’s staying presence.
newtruth: God will never leave me. I can love people without gripping them, and I can face any loss with Him beside me.
prayer2: Lord, thank You for staying with me. Steady my heart and help me to love others freely. Amen.
